## Results

### Data summary

After quality control filtering, 12,163 valid observation-days across
35 calendar years (1986--2025) were available for analysis. The
overall circular mean peak hour was 15:58:00 local time
(circular SD = 2.84 h), confirming that the daily maximum at
Épinal typically occurs in the mid-afternoon, consistent with
boundary-layer heating dynamics.

### Primary trend estimate

The von Mises circular regression yielded a slope of
$-0.0281$ h/decade (95\% bootstrap CI: -0.0699, 0.0121;
$\kappa = 2.45$). This corresponds to approximately $-1.7$ min/decade,
indicating no statistically detectable shift in peak timing over
the study period at the annual scale.

Figure~\ref{fig-wrapped-scatter} shows the daily peak-hour observations
with the fitted von Mises trend line and 95% confidence band. The
hexagonal binning reveals the dominant concentration of peak hours in
the 14:00--18:00 window (approximately $68.7\%$ of observations), with
the broad spread reflecting meteorological day-to-day variability.

![Daily peak-hour observations (hexbin density) with von Mises
  regression trend line and 95% bootstrap confidence band.
  The circular y-axis (0h$\leftrightarrow$24h) is shown zoomed to
  8--22h for readability.](../results/figures/wrapped_scatter.pdf){#fig-wrapped-scatter}

### Sensitivity analyses

All eight pre-registered sensitivity variants produced results
consistent with the primary estimate (Table~\ref{tbl-sensitivity}),
indicating that the trend is not driven by any single methodological
choice.

| Variant | $\beta$ (h/decade) | 95% CI | n obs |
|---------|--------------------|----------|-------|
| Primary (earliest tie) | $-0.0281$ | $(-0.0699, 0.0121)$ | 12,163 |
| Latest tie | $-0.0358$ | $(-0.0784, 0.0054)$ | 12,163 |
| Min years = 20 | $-0.0281$ | $(-0.0699, 0.0121)$ | 12,163 |
| MAD threshold = 3.0 | --- | --- | --- |
| Exclude post-2000 | --- | --- | --- |
| 3-hour subsampling | $-0.0225$ | $(-0.0680, 0.0199)$ | 12,163 |
| 6-hour subsampling | $-0.0536$ | $(-0.1117, 0.0023)$ | 12,163 |
| Min amplitude 1.0°C | $-0.0281$ | $(-0.0699, 0.0121)$ | 12,163 |
| Min amplitude 3.0°C | $-0.0177$ | $(-0.0592, 0.0241)$ | 11,457 |
: Sensitivity analysis results across eight pre-registered variants.
CI bounds are 2.5th and 97.5th bootstrap percentiles. {#tbl-sensitivity}


Figure~\ref{fig-rose-diagram} compares the circular distribution of
peak hours in the early and late halves of the record, showing
a subtle shift in the concentration and direction of peak
hours.

### Seasonal patterns

The year--season interaction LR test was significant ($\chi^2 = 13.71$,
df = 3, $p = 0.0033$), indicating that the year-slope varies by
meteorological season. I therefore report per-season estimates with
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control across the four seasons.

Winter shows a significant advance of $-0.1886$ h/decade
($p = 0.0015$), which survives FDR correction at $\alpha = 0.05$.
Autumn ($+0.0850$ h/decade, $p = 0.10$), spring ($-0.0650$ h/decade,
$p = 0.17$), and summer ($+0.0195$ h/decade, $p = 0.68$) are not
significant after FDR.

| Season | $\beta$ (h/decade) | Wald $p$ | BH rejected |
|--------|--------------------:|:--------:|:-----------:|
| Winter (DJF) | $-0.1886$ | $0.0015$ | Yes |
| Autumn (SON) | $+0.0850$ | $0.10$ | No |
| Spring (MAM) | $-0.0650$ | $0.17$ | No |
| Summer (JJA) | $+0.0195$ | $0.68$ | No |

: Per-season slope estimates from the year--season interaction von
Mises GLM. Wald $p$-values are corrected via the Benjamini-Hochberg
procedure ($\alpha = 0.05$, $m = 4$). Bootstrap CIs are provided in
Table~S1 for reference. {#tbl-seasonal}

Figure~\ref{fig-seasonal} presents the per-season trend panels.

![Seasonal von Mises regression trends. Each panel shows hexbin density
  of daily peak hours and the fitted trend line with 95% CI band.
  ](../results/figures/seasonal_trend.pdf){#fig-seasonal}

### Supplementary analyses

Temperature-weighted von Mises regression (weighting each day by its
diurnal amplitude) produced an estimate of $0.0210$ h/decade
(95\% CI: $-0.0125$ to $0.0528$), which is consistent with the null
of no trend and confirms that the result is not driven by days with
poorly defined peaks. The circular--linear rank correlation (Mardia
1976) yielded $\rho_c = 0.025$ ($p = 0.021$), suggesting a very weak
but statistically detectable association consistent with the small
effect size estimated by the primary MLE model.
